newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa close to resolving pay dispute.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa close to resolving pay dispute.

text.p: Deutsche Lufthansa looked close to the end of a lengthy pay dispute involving some of its staff as their union said on Tuesday it was ready to accept a deal already agreed by other employees at the German flag-carrier.

The DAG white-collar trade union, which represents sections of the ground, air and cockpit staff among the airline's 58,000 workers, said it would accept a wage deal concluded last year by the transport and public sector workers' union OeTV.

"The DAG will accept the wage package agreed between Lufthansa and the OeTV on October 25 last year as part of a wider agreement (on the issue of wages)," a joint union statement signed by DAG chief Roland Issen said.
The 27-month deal signed by OeTV, which represents mainly ground staff, included a 1.8 percent pay rise in 1998, a one-off payment and a share of last year's profits either in cash or shares.

The pact was much less generous than the four percent wage rise which DAG initially demanded. It withdrew from talks late last year to carry out a series of protests that have cost Lufthansa millions of marks in lost business.

Among the conditions of the new wage bargaining structure they proposed, DAG and OeTV said they would seek a "special exemption clause" allowing them to alter future wage agreements in unspecified "significant cases".
They would also seek an increase in the profit-related pay-out currently offered to employees by the airline, the unions added in the statement.
Lufthansa chief executive Juergen Weber welcomed the move and the fact that the two unions would from now on coordinate closely in wage bargaining.
"I am sure that our company will be strengthened by this decision," Weber said in a prepared statement. Talks between Lufthansa and the two unions have been set for April 7.

The background to the union agreement is the fear -- felt by both Lufthansa and its workers -- of increased competition resulting from the liberalisation of Europe's airline markets as from April 1 this year.
Lufthansa is already in the midst of a cost-cutting drive which culminated earlier this year in a decision to remove a layer of its central management and administrative staff.
DAG and OeTV said in their statement that Germany, because of its central position within Europe, was facing "the most serious impact of a ruinous rivalry" in the sector.
Lufthansa has run into conflict with German cartel authorities who argue that it charges too much for domestic German routes such as its Frankfurt-Berlin stretch.
The airline contends that even at current prices such routes are not profitable for it, and so it cannot be charged with abusing its continued dominant position.
